newsitem.title: UK: Tioxide float move surprises ICI analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tioxide float move surprises ICI analysts.

text.p: Imperial Chemical Industries Plc's decision on Thursday to float its Tioxide business on the stock market came as a surprise, analysts said.

Williams de Broe analyst Peter Cartwright said the flotation, pencilled in for the next six to 18 months, "is just the start. The big issue is that they have finally grasped the nettle on restructuring."
Analysts are now predicting a string of disposals, joint ventures and asset swaps in industrial chemicals, with the possibility that ICI could exit completely from some areas.
Kleinwort Benson analyst Jeremy Chantry said the move to realign the company had gained momentum because of a "dynamic in the industry" as a whole.

HSBC James Capel analyst David Ingles said the aim of moving away from industrial chemicals towards the less volatile "light" end of the market in areas like paints, polyurethanes and performance chemicals, "is a worthy objective but it won't be easy. They are selling businesses which are less attractive, to try to buy businesses which are more attractive, and that is a difficult thing to do, especially in terms of shareholder value."
Ingles said that Tioxide Group "won't be an easy company to float. It is a one product business and it is very cyclical."

Kleinwort's Chantry, however, was more upbeat about the move. He said Tioxide Group "is a world number two, which is a nice position to be in," and added there "are considerable barriers" to new players entering the tioxide market, which is highly capital intensive.

There was disappointment over prospects for dividend rises after the ICI suggested that it intended to rebuild its dividend cover. ICI raised its 1996 payout by 6.7 percent, or two pence, to 32.0 pence, at the bottom of forecasts.

"We had been expecting 32 1/2 pence and the the indication is that this (2.0 pence a year) is the ongoing level of dividend increase. That is a slight disappointment," said Ingles. He has reined his 1997 forecast back from 35.0 pence per share to 34.0, and added that yield supprot for the share could be undermined. Chantry has also pencilled in 34.0 pence for 1997, while Cartwright is keeping his forecast at 33.0 pence, expecting the company to be conservative until cover is rebuilt. Ingles said he was maintaining his forecast for 1997 pretax profit before exceptionals at 750 million stg, although he expected "a quite significant exceptional charge."
Ingles said this would result from ICI's continuing efficiency programme.

Cartwright left his 700 million stg figure unchanged, saying "much will depend on how quickly prices recover," while Chantry trimmed his forecast by 50 million stg to 650 million stg on the back of currency worries and likely price pressures in the first half. But he stressed "it is early days yet."
